source_refs.note: Exercise 14.4 Q9, book p.290 (PDF 295). No key answer (proof); identity checked symbolically with sympy. Printed 'vector' for 'vectors'. Solution book PDF 1283-1284 agrees.

blocks.prompt: 9 Prove that for any three non-zero vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\): \((\underline{u} + \underline{v}) \cdot [(\underline{v} + \underline{w}) \times (\underline{w} + \underline{u})] = 2[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof by expanding products of sums.
We must show the left side reduces to \(2[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\).
Plan: expand the cross product, drop the zero terms, then expand the dot product and use: a triple product with a repeated vector is 0, and the cyclic property.
steps:
Given: any vectors \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w}\).
To prove: \((\underline{u} + \underline{v}) \cdot [(\underline{v} + \underline{w}) \times (\underline{w} + \underline{u})] = 2[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\).
Method: distributive laws for \(\times\) and \(\cdot\); \(\underline{w} \times \underline{w} = \underline{0}\); \([\underline{a}\ \underline{a}\ \underline{b}] = 0\); cyclic property.

Expand the cross product
\[(\underline{v} + \underline{w}) \times (\underline{w} + \underline{u})\]
\[= \underline{v} \times \underline{w} + \underline{v} \times \underline{u} + \underline{w} \times \underline{w} + \underline{w} \times \underline{u}\]
\[= \underline{v} \times \underline{w} + \underline{v} \times \underline{u} + \underline{w} \times \underline{u}\]
Why: The cross product distributes over addition (keep the order in each term). \(\underline{w} \times \underline{w} = \underline{0}\) because a vector is parallel to itself.

Dot with \(\underline{u}\)
\[\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{w}) + \underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{u}) + \underline{u} \cdot (\underline{w} \times \underline{u})\]
\[= [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] + 0 + 0\]
Why: \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) and \(\underline{w} \times \underline{u}\) are perpendicular to \(\underline{u}\), so their dot with \(\underline{u}\) is 0 (a repeated vector).

Dot with \(\underline{v}\)
\[\underline{v} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{w}) + \underline{v} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{u}) + \underline{v} \cdot (\underline{w} \times \underline{u})\]
\[= 0 + 0 + [\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}]\]
Why: The first two contain \(\underline{v}\) twice, so they are 0.

Add the two parts
\[\text{L.H.S.} = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] + [\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}]\]
\[= [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] + [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\]
\[= 2[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: \([\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}] = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\) by the cyclic property.

Check with numbers
\[\underline{u} = \underline{i},\ \underline{v} = \underline{j},\ \underline{w} = \underline{k}:\]
\[(\underline{i} + \underline{j}) \cdot [(\underline{j} + \underline{k}) \times (\underline{k} + \underline{i})]\]
\[(\underline{j} + \underline{k}) \times (\underline{k} + \underline{i}) = \underline{i} + \underline{j} - \underline{k}\]
\[(\underline{i} + \underline{j}) \cdot (\underline{i} + \underline{j} - \underline{k}) = 2 = 2[\underline{i}\ \underline{j}\ \underline{k}] \;\checkmark\]
Why: A quick example agrees with the identity.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "for any three non-zero vector"; it should read "vectors". The identity itself is correct (it even holds for zero vectors).
